newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's BM&F seeks freer access for foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's BM&F seeks freer access for foreigners.

text.p: Brazil's BM&F futures exchange and the country's Central Bank are discussing allowing foreign investors freer access to trade agricultural and overseas debt contracts, the BM&F's president said.

"In the same way Brazilians can go freely to the Chicago futures market, we want foreigners to be able to do the same thing in Brazil. Nothing more than that," Manoel Felix Cintra Neto told a press conference in Rio de Janeiro.
Foreign investors can currently trade on all contracts at the Sao Paulo-based exchange but only by means of set instruments such as a Central Bank regulated account.
One month ago Brazil's National Monetary Council (CMN) movedto allow foreign investors to operate more freely by authorisingtrading in derivatives markets for hedging purposes under Annex Four rules.

In the case of the BM&F however, the need for a physical position to justify the hedge effectively means foreign investors can only benefit from the change if they trade on the interest rates futures, stock market index and the dollar futures contracts, traders said.
Any change which might directly benefit other contracts would be welcomed, dealers said.

"We welcome any type of opening of the local market for foreign investors as we have seen a great deal of overseas interest in recent years," said Michael McDougall, director of commodities futures at Fimat Futures.
Cintra Neto said he has optimistic that the issue would be decided in the next two months.
"I am very optimisitic...I expect that at the very most everything will be resolved in 60 days," Cintro Neto.
The BM&F is the world's fourth largest futures exchange in terms of contracts traded. In 1996 financial volume surged to $4.7 trillion, up more than 50 percent from roughly $3.0 trillion in 1995.
The number of contracts fell nine percent to 136 million but this was due to a change in the size of contracts last year.

Interest rate contracts accounted for 62 percent of financial volume in 1996, exchange rate contracts 20 percent, swaps seven percent, stock index contracts six percent, options three percent and agriculture, gold and others one percent.

In the first half of this year, around 60 million contracts were traded, down from 70 million in January to June last year although this was again due to the change in contract size, Cintra Nero said.
Daily financial volume rose to $25 billion from $15 billion in the first half of 1996, he added.
The discussions with the Central Bank are part of the BM&F's drive to internationalise both the exchange's contracts and the exchange.
In the case of the bourse itself, BM&F officials have been holding talks with officials from other Mercosur countries about creating a Mercosur exchange.
While futures exchanges also exist in other Mercosur countries, the BM&F is "the most developed", Cintra Neto said.
Cintra Neto said he hoped to have talked to all the other exchanges in Mercosur countries by August and that a decision would be taken in November.
